title: Beauty Giants "Move House" at CIIE: Labs and Innovation Chains Land in China as Niche Brands Squeeze Through the Narrow Door - BigGo Finance

 Add preferred source At the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), international beauty groups including L'Oréal, Estée Lauder and Shiseido shifted their focus from new product debuts to local R&D, supply chains and open innovation platforms, landing laboratories, co-creation programs and investment projects in China and arguing that the country is transforming from a commercial market into a source of innovation. L'Oréal took a minority stake in PAM2L Biotechnologies, and its sunscreen filter Mexoryl 400, co-developed with BASF, won approval in China. Estée Lauder unveiled a skin longevity science platform and deepened AI cooperation with Alibaba Cloud. Meanwhile, niche brands such as BeauEver used the expo to seek opportunities in segmented categories. In the first three quarters of 2026, retail sales of cosmetics above the designated size totaled 349.1 billion yuan (approximately $52.4 billion), up 6.1% year on year, outpacing overall retail sales. Key Elements 
 China International Import Expo (CIIE) L'Oréal Estée Lauder Shiseido Nicolas Hieronimus Stéphane de La Faverie Toshinobu Umetsu PAM2L Biotechnologies Beauty X BeauEver Procter & Gamble BASF Mexoryl 400 Boao Lecheng The consumer goods section of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) has stayed crowded since opening, with the beauty and personal care zone particularly packed. Unlike previous editions, international beauty groups this year placed R&D capabilities, local supply chains and open innovation platforms ahead of new product launches in both their booth displays and executive remarks. The shift from "selling products to China" to "putting projects in China and bringing Chinese experience to the world" has become the clearest storyline in the beauty segment at this year's expo.
 L'Oréal Group Chief Executive Officer Nicolas Hieronimus attended in person for the second time this year. Speaking at a group media briefing, he said China is L'Oréal's second-largest market globally and the group will continue investing in talent and facilities in the country. China is also an important innovation engine, he said, with local consumers growing more sophisticated and raising their demands on products, forcing companies to accelerate their innovation pace. He highlighted collaboration between the Pudong laboratory and the local startup ecosystem, saying the results would serve not only the Chinese market but also the world. At this year's CIIE, L'Oréal brought five new brands and a series of innovations, with its booth themed "Odyssey of Beauty," showcasing 27 brands, five global debuts and more than 10 China debuts.
 Estée Lauder Companies put its "science wall" at the center of its booth. President and Chief Executive Officer Stéphane de La Faverie said at the opening ceremony that China has become one of the world's most vibrant and mature beauty markets and offers an important template for the group's next phase of accelerated growth, adding that the company's commitment to China is long-term. During the expo, Estée Lauder launched its "Leading Skin Longevity" scientific innovation platform, with skin longevity science laboratories in Melville, in the United States, and Shanghai. De La Faverie said China is at the forefront of science and consumer innovation and that the group is honored to launch the platform there.
 Shiseido China and Travel Retail CEO Toshinobu Umetsu summarized the group's innovation path in China in three stages: in the past, it brought global innovation to China; now it creates together with local Chinese teams; and going forward, Chinese teams are able to incubate global-caliber innovation on their own. He said plainly that China is not just a business market but Shiseido's source of innovation. At this year's CIIE, Shiseido's booth showcased more than 60 products and cutting-edge results spanning skin science and hair regeneration medical technology. The group also announced a strategic partnership with Hainan Qiyan Stem Cell Anti-Aging Hospital, leveraging the policy advantages of the Boao Lecheng pilot zone to advance feasibility exploration and full-chain application of innovative hair regeneration.
 Judging from booth content, international brands have clearly increased their investment in the "anti-aging" narrative. Estée Lauder used a "skin longevity clock" installation to explain the synergy among multiple aging hallmarks, while Shiseido "moved" its China R&D center to the venue, breaking down research on the life cycle of pigmentation, the causes of deep wrinkles and collagen mechanics into visual charts. In a market where the population over 60 exceeds 300 million, anti-aging is no longer just a marketing term but an actual direction of R&D spending.
 Alongside scientific displays, the brands are connecting with China's local innovation ecosystem. L'Oréal announced a minority investment in PAM2L Biotechnologies, a Chinese AI-native biomaterials R&D and application company. The two sides will jointly develop innovative bioactive ingredients and promote their application in beauty, with the investment made through the open innovation investment arm of L'Oréal China's Beauty Tech venture unit and supported by the group's BOLD strategic innovation venture capital fund. Hieronimus disclosed that an ingredient developed by PAM2L called Colayin will soon be used in several of the group's brands, while the L'Oréal Professionnel AirLight Pro hair dryer is the result of joint development with Chinese startup Ruyuan Technology.
 There has also been substantive progress in raw materials and scientific collaboration. Mexoryl 400, a sunscreen filter co-developed by L'Oréal and BASF and used exclusively by L'Oréal Group, has been approved for registration in China, becoming the first sunscreen filter approved since the Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Cosmetics took effect. Three products in the La Roche-Posay "Anthelios" sunscreen line that use the ingredient were approved for registration at the same time. L'Oréal China also established a "Skin Barrier Innovation and Translation Joint Laboratory" with the Shanghai Skin Disease Hospital to study the skin barrier characteristics of Chinese populations, with CeraVe serving as the core vehicle for translating the results.
 Open innovation platforms are becoming a common route for international groups to connect with local startups. Estée Lauder's Beauty X program has attracted more than 1,000 startups and teams since its launch in 2024, and this year it awarded eight winning companies, six of which have begun order cooperation with the group. The world's first recombinant salmon PDRN product went from project matchmaking to market launch in just nine months. L'Oréal's BIG BANG Beauty Tech Creative Camp this year unveiled 22 winning companies, bringing together innovation from North Asia and France and plugging startup technologies directly into the group's business chain. In addition, Estée Lauder Companies and Alibaba Cloud Intelligence signed a strategic cooperation memorandum at the CIIE venue to further deepen cooperation in artificial intelligence.
 As the giants ramp up R&D, another group of smaller exhibitors is looking for its own place. Global Empowerment Group CEO Zheng Ke brought only one brand, BeauEver, to the expo last year; this year he moved all four of the group's brands into the CIIE venue. He said the expo lets more people see new brands, that China's consumer market is large enough, and that after years of skincare consumers clearly know what suits them, so as long as a brand cuts precisely enough into a segmented category, there will certainly be growth opportunities. BeauEver this year co-created products with a New Zealand skier, offering sunscreen lotion, sunscreen sticks and sunscreen lip balm to meet the needs of application before exercise, reapplication along the way and lip protection, and incorporated cleansing, moisturizing and rest into its product line.
 Overall market data leave room for imagination for new brands. Data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show that from January to September 2026, retail sales of cosmetics above the designated size reached 349.1 billion yuan (approximately $52.4 billion), up 6.1% year on year, outpacing total retail sales of consumer goods by 5 percentage points. In the first half, retail sales of cosmetics by units above the designated size were 244.5 billion yuan (approximately $36.7 billion), up 6.3% year on year, while total retail sales grew 1.3% over the same period; in June alone, cosmetics growth rose to 12.6%. The industry has shifted from rapid growth to a stage of steady development, and structural divergence under stock competition has become the core feature of this year's beauty market: high-end international brands are making a strong comeback, leading Chinese domestic brands are achieving structural breakthroughs through multi-brand matrices, and segments such as functional skincare and skin science care continue to expand.
 The performance of foreign groups supports their increased investment in local innovation. L'Oréal's latest data for the period ended September 30 show sales rose 6.9% year on year on an adjusted basis in the first three quarters, with China the main engine driving growth in North Asia; with the overall market growing at a low single-digit rate and growth driven mainly by the premium beauty market, L'Oréal's growth in China was close to three times the overall market rate. Hieronimus said the main reason behind the results is advancing innovation faster and with higher quality, a lesson learned from China and a direction the group must keep pursuing around the world.
 Judging from the exhibition halls, the display logic of international beauty giants has already changed: new product walls representing sales have given way to science walls representing the future, and simple product trade has given way to the integrated landing of laboratories, supply chains and investment projects. For new faces, the CIIE is still a door that can be knocked on, but the competition behind that door is shifting from channels and marketing to depth of R&D and speed of local response.
